overview:
In April 1526 a Timurid prince from Ferghana named Babur, who had already lost Samarkand more than once and made a base for himself at Kabul, met the far larger army of the Delhi sultan Ibrahim Lodi on the plain at Panipat north of Delhi. His field artillery and matchlockmen, screened behind a line of lashed carts, broke the Lodi centre, and within days Delhi and Agra were his. What followed was less a conquest than a long, contested settling-in. Babur's own memoirs record the unease of a Central Asian army camped among people it did not understand, and the messy fighting of that first summer — a force sent across the Ganges to relieve Sambhal, where a Mughal commander took the town by a ruse rather than a storm — is more typical of the period than Panipat's clean drama. Afghan resistance regrouped under Ibrahim's brother Mahmud Lodi with backing from the sultan of Bengal, and only at the Ghaghra river in Bihar in 1529, in the last campaign of Babur's life, was organised opposition in the north broken. His son Humayun then lost the whole inheritance to the Afghan Sher Shah Suri and spent years in Persian exile before recovering it in 1555, dying a few months later.

The empire that historians actually mean by "Mughal" was built by Humayun's son Akbar over a reign of nearly fifty years. He put in place the mansabdari system, which graded officers by numerical rank and tied their pay to assigned revenue, and the zabt settlement, which assessed land tax in cash against measured yields — instruments that let a court at Agra or Lahore extract from provinces a thousand miles away. He also drew Rajput houses into the ruling elite by marriage and office, and abolished the tax on non-Muslims, which made his court unusually broad for its time. Expansion east continued under his generals: the defeat of the Afghan sultan Daud Khan Karrani at Tukaroi in Odisha in 1575 shattered the Bengal Sultanate, and Bengal — which had gone its own way since the 1330s — was absorbed the following year. By the seventeenth century the empire spanned most of the subcontinent, and the Indian economy it governed was among the largest in the world, with Bengal's cotton and silk supplying Dutch, English and Armenian merchants who came for textiles and paid in silver from the Americas. Shah Jahan's building programme, the Taj Mahal above all, and the painting workshops that flourished from Akbar onward, belong to the same fiscal machine.

Aurangzeb pushed the frontiers to their furthest extent in the Deccan and left them exhausted. After his death in 1707 the succession fractured, provincial governors in Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad became rulers in fact, the Marathas took tribute from much of the interior, and Nadir Shah's sack of Delhi in 1739 carried off the treasury and the peacock throne. The dynasty survived another century mostly as a legitimating name: the English East India Company took the revenue rights of Bengal and Bihar in 1765 and ruled in the emperor's name long after it had stopped obeying him. When the rebellion of 1857 made the aged Bahadur Shah Zafar its figurehead, the British deposed him, tried him, and exiled him to Rangoon.
significance: More than any earlier state in South Asia, the Mughal empire fixed what "India" meant as a political unit — a single revenue administration, a shared court language in Persian, and an imperial idea that its successors, including the British Raj and to some degree the modern republic, inherited rather than invented. Its fiscal and land-settlement records became the raw material of colonial revenue systems and, later, of the long argument among historians about whether India was drained or developed by British rule. Culturally its reach is still visible in Urdu, in Hindustani music, in the domed-and-arched architecture that anchors Delhi, Agra and Lahore, and in miniature painting. It is also politically live: Akbar's accommodation of non-Muslim subjects and Aurangzeb's reversal of it are argued over in India today with a heat that has more to do with the present than the seventeenth century.
coverage: Written from Wikipedia and Britannica overviews plus searches on the specific battles; the four events this dataset holds are all early military engagements from Babur's and Akbar's conquests, so the administrative, economic and cultural life that made the empire matter is not represented in them at all, and nothing after 1575 is. In the wider record, the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries are unusually well documented by court chronicles and memoirs — but those are official, Persian-language and written for the emperor, so peasant, regional and non-Muslim perspectives survive far more thinly; small engagements like the 1526 Sambhal episode rest on brief passages in Babur's memoirs and later compilations, and details such as troop numbers at Panipat are estimates, not counts.
